In [[mathematics]], a [[linear operator]] <math>f: V\to V</math> is called '''locally finite''' if the [[linear space|space]] <math>V</math> is the union of a family of finite-dimensional <math>f</math>-[[invariant subspace]]s.<ref>{{cite arXiv|title=Central Simple Poisson Algebras|author1=Yucai Su|author2=Xiaoping Xu|eprint=math/0011086v1|year=2000 }}</ref><ref name=ControlBk>{{cite book|title=Time-Varying Systems and Computations|first1=Patrick|last1=DeWilde|first2=Alle-Jan|last2=van&nbsp;der&nbsp;Veen|publisher=Springer Science+Business Media, B.V.|isbn=978-1-4757-2817-0|doi=10.1007/978-1-4757-2817-0|year=1998|location=Dordrecht}}</ref>{{rp|40}}

In other words, there exists a family <math>\{ V_i\vert i\in I\}</math> of linear subspaces of <math>V</math>,  such that we have the following:
* <math>\bigcup_{i\in I} V_i=V</math>
* <math>(\forall i\in I) f[V_i]\subseteq V_i</math>
* Each <math>V_i</math> is finite-dimensional.

An equivalent condition only requires <math>V</math> to be spanned by finite-dimensional <math>f</math>-invariant subspaces.<ref name=Radford>{{cite journal|title=Operators on Hopf Algebras|first=David&nbsp;E.|last=Radford|journal=American Journal of Mathematics|date=Feb 1977|volume=99|number=1|pages=139–158|publisher=Johns Hopkins University Press|doi=10.2307/2374012 |jstor=2374012}}</ref><ref name=ControlProc>{{cite conference|title=On the Riccati Equations of the ''H''<sup>∞</sup> Control Problem for Discrete Time-Varying Systems|first1=Jacquelien|last1=Scherpen|first2=Michel |last2=Verhaegen|conference=3rd European Control Conference (Rome, Italy)|date=September 1995|citeseerx=10.1.1.867.5629 }}</ref>  If <math>V</math> is also a [[Hilbert space]], sometimes an operator is called locally finite when the sum of the <math>\{ V_i\vert i\in I\}</math> is only [[dense set|dense]] in <math>V</math>.<ref name=ControlBk />{{rp|78–79}}

==Examples==
* Every linear operator on a finite-dimensional space is trivially locally finite.
* Every [[diagonalizable]] (i.e. there exists a [[Basis (linear algebra)|basis]] of <math>V</math> whose elements are all [[eigenvector]]s of <math>f</math>) linear operator is locally finite, because it is the union of subspaces spanned by finitely many eigenvectors of <math>f</math>.
* The operator on <math>\mathbb{C}[x]</math>, the space of polynomials with complex coefficients, defined by <math>T(f(x))=xf(x)</math>, is ''not'' locally finite; any <math>T</math>-invariant subspace is of the form <math>\mathbb{C}[x]f_0(x)</math> for some <math>f_0(x)\in\mathbb{C}[x]</math>, and so has infinite (or zero) dimension.  
* The operator on <math>\mathbb{C}[x]</math> defined by <math>T(f(x))=\frac{f(x)-f(0)}{x}</math> is locally finite; for any <math>n</math>, the polynomials of [[degree (polynomials)|degree]] at most <math>n</math> form a <math>T</math>-invariant subspace.<ref>[https://math.stackexchange.com/users/431940/joppy Joppy] (Apr 28, 2018), [https://math.stackexchange.com/a/2757511/330413 answer] to "[https://math.stackexchange.com/q/2757511 Locally Finite Operator]".  ''Mathematics StackExchange''.  [[StackExchange|StackOverflow]].</ref>
